t: You are the manager, not the technician
p: Default sequence: assess → communicate → prioritize → document → act.
You advise, recommend, and escalate. The owner decides.
If your answer jumps to the technical fix, it is usually wrong.
What is the business objective?
Who owns the decision?
What is the first management step?
What is the cost–benefit logic?
What process should be followed?
FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST change the answer.
Several options may be things you would eventually do — only one is credited.
Colon-form stems: options complete the sentence.
Role effectiveness → existing proficiencies, not management support.
Security early in a project → feasibility, not cost.
Awareness metric → number of reported incidents.
Classification → consequences of compromise, not risk.
Highest response priority → life safety.
The broadest correct answer wins (business objectives ⊃ legal obligations).
Absolutes — always, never, all — are usually wrong.
If any part of an option is wrong, the whole option is wrong.
Two near-identical options → neither; two opposites → one of them.
Strategy → policy → program → budgets → procedures. Each derives from the one above.
Legal and regulatory requirements are constraints, not the driver.
First step in developing strategy: review business objectives.
Board and senior management are ultimately accountable; it cannot be delegated.
The manager develops the strategy; senior management approves it.
Data owners decide and confirm access to their data.
Governance implementation FIRST requires approved policy.
Policies are based on a threat profile — proportionate protection.
Standards: measurable requirements. Procedures: unambiguous, meet standards. Guidelines: advisory.
Strategic alignment · Risk management · Value delivery
Resource management · Performance measurement · Assurance process integration
Value delivery = investment optimized to support objectives.

t: Win commitment with outcomes, not fear
p: Show how security supports desired business outcomes.
A business case, not attack statistics, wins funding.
Commitment shows as resources and participation, not signatures.
What most inhibits governance: lack of high-level sponsorship.
Board: risk trends relative to appetite, in business terms.
Governance metrics are strategic — expense against projected outcomes.
KGI = goal achieved · KPI = process performance · KRI = risk rising.
Objective: risk at an acceptable level — not the lowest possible.
Acceptability is set by organizational requirements; appetite by senior management.
A risk already within appetite is accepted and monitored.

t: Assess, then hand the decision to the owner
p: High risk found → report to the risk owner FIRST.
The business owner accepts residual risk; security never does.
Risk beyond appetite and unfunded → escalate with a business impact analysis.
Threat = actor/event · Vulnerability = weakness · Risk = the combination · Impact = consequence.
Inherent = before controls · Residual = after controls.
Appetite = strategic willingness · Tolerance = acceptable variation.
Disruption from DDoS = operational risk.
Analysis addresses size AND likelihood of loss.
Not complete until evaluated against appetite and tolerance.
Residual risk is determined by a risk assessment.
Best process for existing risk level: a security review.

t: Cost–benefit with total cost of ownership
p: A control should not cost more than the exposure it addresses.
Compare with life-cycle cost, not purchase price.
Vulnerabilities are evaluated for threat, impact, and cost of mitigation.
Continuous monitoring and KRIs catch change between assessments.
When risk changes, standards and procedures change; policies should not need to.
Reassess on significant change. Treat regulation as another risk.

t: Executive commitment is the #1 success factor
p: Ahead of policies, communication, and training.
The perennial challenges: management support, funding, staffing.
A technical, tactically driven program signals weak management components.
Inventory → classification → owners → baselines → controls → metrics.
Prerequisite to classification: impact assessment.
Classification reflects consequences of compromise, not risk.
DLP starts with classifying data, not buying a tool.

t: Technology implements controls — it is not one
p: Preventive · detective · corrective · deterrent · compensating.
A countermeasure is targeted at a specific threat; a general control is broader.
Effectiveness is proven by testing against the objective.
Preventive control objectives derive from risk levels aligned with appetite.
Awareness effectiveness: number of reported incidents (rising is good).
100% completion with rising incidents = training isn't working.
Define the decisions metrics support before choosing metrics.
Establish program metrics in the design phase.
Least privilege limits impact of compromise.
Recertification cures privilege creep; segregation of duties stops one-person fraud.
Automatic expiry removes contractor access; RBAC prevents internal modification.
Screening depth matches role sensitivity.
Requirements go in the RFP and contract from the start.
The SLA is the most encompassing contractual element.
Independent audit reports give assurance; accountability is retained.
Never let an outsourced service become a single point of failure.
IDS for internet traffic → screened subnet; most important consideration → tuning.
Network DoS → packet filtering.
OS weaknesses → patch management.
Baseline controls: RBAC, logging, automated patching (not mirroring).

t: Confirm → classify → contain → eradicate → recover → learn
p: A reported breach is confirmed before anything else.
Active, spreading damage: contain now.
Eradicate before recovering, or you reinfect.
Roles, escalation, and communication procedures are the plan's core.
Severity criteria are predefined and live in the manual.
Delegate authority to act — needing an unreachable executive's approval is the flaw.
Cross-functional team: legal, HR, communications, business.
Involve managers from affected operational areas.
Strategic triage is by business impact; triage exists to prioritize limited resources.
Life safety first — before continuity, recovery, or messaging.
RTO = time to restore · RPO = max data loss · SDO = minimum service level · AIW/MTO = max tolerable outage.
RTO must fit within the AIW. A stricter RPO can make the RTO unattainable.
Site tier is chosen by RTO against cost; alternate site must not share the primary's hazards.
Disclosure and ransom: senior management with legal counsel.
Regulatory notification: engage legal first.
Insider incidents: HR and legal before acting.
A designated spokesperson handles media.
Chain of custody whenever evidence may be used legally.
Forensic copy = bit-by-bit image.
Administrators confirm and scope — and alter nothing.
Root compromise → rebuild from original media.
Post-incident review exists to improve the process; blameless; actions tracked to closure.
Most common DR plan failure: stale operational information.
A DR test succeeds when critical business processes are duplicated — not merely when the RTO is met.
